{"sample_id": "blind-733d658815c94eb68a74692ecec6c298", "theorem": "Define $f_{n}:[0,1] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ by the equation $f_{n}(x)=x^{n}$. Show that the sequence $\left(f_{n}\right)$ does not converge uniformly.", "assumptions": [], "domain": "topology", "explicit_subgoals": [], "candidate_text": "For each \(x\in[0,1)\), \(x^n\to0\), while \(f_n(1)=1\) for every \(n\). Thus the pointwise limit is
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&0\le x<1,\\1,&x=1.\end{cases}
\]
Any uniform limit would necessarily equal this pointwise limit. Fix \(\varepsilon=\tfrac12\). For every \(N\in\mathbb Z_+\), take \(n=N\) and \(x=2^{-1/N}<1\). Then
\[
|f_n(x)-f(x)|=x^n=\left(2^{-1/N}\right)^N=\tfrac12.
\]
Hence for every \(N\) there exist \(n\ge N\) and \(x\in[0,1]\) such that \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|\ge\varepsilon\). Therefore \((f_n)\) does not converge uniformly on \([0,1]\)."}

{"sample_id": "blind-89dfed01509d4f8b82c222d2bdbbb3fe", "theorem": "Prove that any two nonabelian groups of order 21 are isomorphic.", "assumptions": [], "domain": "abstract_algebra", "explicit_subgoals": [], "candidate_text": "\begin{proof}

    By Cauchy's theorem we have that if $G$ is a group of order 21 then it has an element $a$ of order 3 and an element $b$ of order 7. By exercise 2.5.41 we have that the subgroup generated by $b$ is normal, so there is some $i=0,1,2,3,4,5,6$ such that $a b a^{-1}=b^i$. We know $i \neq$ 0 since that implies $a b=a$ and so that $b=e$, a contradiction, and we know $i \neq 1$ since then $a b=b a$ and this would imply $G$ is abelian, which we are assuming is not the case.

Now, $a$ has order 3 so we must have $b=a^3 b a^{-3}=b^{i^3}$ mod 7 , and so $i$ is restricted by the modular equation $i^3 \equiv 1 \bmod 7$

\begin{center}

\begin{tabular}{|c|c|}

\hline$x$ & $x^3 \bmod 7$ \\

\hline 2 & 1 \\

\hline 3 & 6 \\

\hline 4 & 1 \\

\hline 5 & 6 \\

\hline 6 & 6 \\

\hline

\end{tabular}

\end{center}

Therefore the only options are $i=2$ and $i=4$. Now suppose $G$ is such that $a b a^{-1}=b^2$ and let $G^{\prime}$ be another group of order 21 with an element $c$ of order 3 and an element $d$ of order 7 such that $c d c^{-1}=d^4$. We now prove that $G$ and $G^{\prime}$ are isomorphic. Define

$$

\begin{aligned}

\phi: G & \rightarrow G^{\prime} \\

a & \mapsto c^{-1} \\

b & \mapsto d

\end{aligned}

$$
